reading.body:
Defense AI procurement is documented in free federal databases, SAM.gov, USAspending, and FPDS, with the Defense Innovation Unit as the commercial entry point and subscription analysts layered on top.

The free sources are the primary record. SAM.gov lists solicitations and awards, USAspending carries every federal award, and FPDS records contract actions and vendor performance at the transaction level. DIU is where commercial AI enters DoD programs, with public project listings. Govini builds decision science on that record, and Silicon Valley Defense Group maps the commercial entrants.

The programs of record are decision support, autonomy, and ISR processing, the AI applications the sector tracks. Tracking them through procurement data shows actual spending and vendor capability, not just announcements. What the data does not show is compute demand, building capacity, or power requirements, none of those appear in these sources. Government AI labs are catalogued separately, not here.

summary: Decision support, autonomy, and ISR processing are the programs of record; DIU is the commercial on-ramp. Who tracks the sector: free government procurement databases are the primary record, with dedicated defense-intelligence firms layered on top - this page starts with the sources anyone can verify.

analysis.body:
The material available for defense does not include an official Census Bureau adoption figure, so there is no measured adoption rate to report here. What the sources do show is the machinery through which AI enters the sector and how that entry can be observed. Per SAM.gov, the government's own system of record, federal contract opportunities, awards, and subcontract reports are searchable there, and per FPDS, the Federal Procurement Data System records contract actions and vendor performance history at the transaction level. USAspending carries the award data, downloadable, built on the Federal Procurement Data System feed. For anyone trying to size AI activity in defense, these three systems are the primary evidence, and all of them are free to search.

The commercial on-ramp is named explicitly. The Defense Innovation Unit is described as where commercial AI enters DoD programs, with public project listings, and its stated mission is to convert entrepreneurial products into tangible combat power. The curated points describe DIU as the commercial gateway, and the Silicon Valley Defense Group is described as a nonprofit that monitors the intersection of commercial tech, private capital, and national security, publicly mapping the companies driving AI adoption in the DoD space. Between the two, a reader can see both the government's intake point and an outside map of the vendors approaching it.

On the vendor and analytics side, Govini is described as a defense-intelligence platform used inside the Department that tracks procurement trends, supply-chain risk, and vendor capability in AI and autonomy, and that publishes public scorecards on critical-technology spending. Its own page describes a platform layer that transforms activated data into adaptive workflows, mobilized agents, and AI-driven orchestration that proactively forecasts issues, prioritizes recommendations, and aligns resources. Janes is described as a long-running defense analysis provider maintaining databases of contractors, programs, and procurement forecasts, a subscription source, and its page describes validated, peer-reviewed intelligence drawing on human collectors as well as data. These are the sources that turn the raw procurement record into trend analysis.

The curated points frame what this page covers as decision support, autonomy, and ISR processing as programs of record, with DIU as the commercial on-ramp and free federal procurement data placed first and subscription analysts labeled. That ordering is itself the practical guidance: the free record is the starting point, and the paid analysts are supplementary. The Government Labs section of this site catalogues government AI research organisations, listing two verified entries, Technology Innovation Institute in Abu Dhabi and Shanghai AI Laboratory in China, both state-funded and drawing on sovereign budgets rather than venture capital or product revenue. That is context on the government-lab model rather than on United States defense procurement specifically.

On ROI, the sources are largely silent. No excerpt reports a return figure, a cost saving, or a performance improvement attributable to AI in defense programs. Govini's page claims forecasting and prioritization benefits in general terms, and DIU states its mission in terms of combat power, but neither offers measured outcomes. A reader should treat the absence as an absence, not as evidence either way.

On risk and regulation, the material is procedural rather than policy-driven. SAM.gov notes that the system contains Controlled Unclassified Information and that viewing, reproducing, or disposing of it must follow 32 CFR Part 2002 and GSA Order CIO 2103.2 CUI Policy, and that the system is for official use only and subject to monitoring. FPDS carries the same official-use and monitoring notice. The procurement infrastructure itself is in transition: per SAM.gov, the FPDS.gov ezSearch feature has been retired and all contract award data searches should be conducted in SAM.gov, with the FPDS.gov ATOM Feed to be retired later in FY 2026, and per FPDS, the General Services Administration has retired the Electronic Subcontracting Reporting System with subcontracting reporting now available in SAM.gov. SAM.gov also notes that revisions to ISR eligibility logic in the Subcontracting Plan Reporting system on June 9, 2026 may cause contractors to see an increased volume of contracts and subcontracts in their Eligible Workspace, and that this inclusion does not automatically carry a further obligation.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the takeaway from this material is about where to look rather than what to buy. The federal procurement record on SAM.gov, FPDS, and USAspending is the auditable trail of what the Department has actually bought, and DIU is the named entry point for commercial products. The subscription analysts, Janes among them, exist to interpret that trail. Nothing in these sources establishes a measured adoption rate, a demonstrated return, or a specific regulatory constraint on AI deployment in defense beyond the handling rules for controlled unclassified information and the ongoing consolidation of procurement systems.

https://www.svdg.org/.brief: The page presents Motiv, an agency run by Andrej Schindler and Jonas von der Gathen that describes itself as an "Agentur für Zukunftspotenziale", placing creative people with values-oriented companies. It says it connects people and companies, accompanies individual development and creates space for future perspectives, driven by curiosity about people and how organisations evolve. Companies are described as grown, unique organisms whose sense of purpose and urge to develop are their driving forces, and the agency says its aim is to place people who bring both professional expertise and the ability to connect with a company's purpose. It states that it works with companies holding social and ecological values and seeks long-term working relationships, and that it sees people as developing beings whose individual potential it tries to recognise at the right moment for a career step. The page also invites readers to register for a quarterly newsletter with open positions, accounts of company visits and interviews.

https://www.janes.com/.brief: Janes reports that it gathers information from vetted on-ground specialists, exclusive interviews, and events, acting as human sensors that web crawlers cannot reach. Janes reports that every data point is verified against reliable, vetted sources and that its dataset is the largest of its type, connecting millions of points to uncover patterns. Janes reports that its final content is peer reviewed to meet its quality and accuracy standards, and that it supplies validated data for the Joint Intelligence Preparation of the Operational Environment process. Janes reports that its digital portal lets users navigate validated data to uncover insights, moving from “what happened” to “what it means.”

https://www.govini.com/.brief: Govini says that Air is a leader in Enterprise Readiness and that its mission is to make readiness a real-time, continuously achieved condition. The company explains that its platform layer turns activated data into adaptive workflows, mobilized agents, and AI-driven orchestration that forecasts issues, prioritizes recommendations, and aligns resources.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/ec.brief: The page catalogues two organisations it classifies as government AI labs, each verified individually against a document the organisation published about itself, with the deciding source and the date it was last read recorded. It states that Shanghai AI Laboratory is a state-established Chinese research institution backed by national ministries and the Shanghai municipal government, and that the Technology Innovation Institute in Abu Dhabi operates under that emirate's Advanced Technology Research Council and has published frontier open models. The page argues that state-funded labs hold a distinct position because they carry public mandates and draw on sovereign budgets rather than venture capital or product revenue, which it says shapes what they build and why. It adds that both institutions can in principle command infrastructure commitments, including compute and facilities, that market-driven labs must negotiate for commercially.
